Could you quote exactly what Pinocchio tells himself about following the pipes today and going to school tomorrow? My sister is covering my chores for a course I'm taking; I picture making it up to her when I qualify, but I keep wasting the study evenings she gives me. Can we look at that gap without turning it into 'I'm a terrible person'?

context_resolution.explanation: The reader explicitly confirmed this completed chapter in the current message.

observed.reply:
In Chapter 9, Pinocchio tells himself:

“Today I’ll follow the pipes, and tomorrow I’ll go to school. There’s
always plenty of time to go to school,”

The line captures a gap between a sincere larger intention and the small decision that postpones it. Your situation sounds worth examining in that same practical register—not as proof that you’re a terrible person, but as a pattern: your sister’s help creates study time, you picture a future way of repaying it, and then some of those evenings slip away.

A useful question might be: **when one of those evenings goes off course, what are you choosing in the moment instead of studying—and what would make beginning feel easier without turning the evening into a test of your character?**

evidence.location: Chapter 9 — Pinocchio sells his A-B-C book to pay his way into the Marionette Theater., source lines 897-939
evidence.text:
See Pinocchio hurrying off to school with his new A-B-C book under
his arm! As he walked along, his brain was busy planning hundreds of
wonderful things, building hundreds of castles in the air. Talking to
himself, he said:

“In school today, I’ll learn to read, tomorrow to write, and the day
after tomorrow I’ll do arithmetic. Then, clever as I am, I can earn a
lot of money. With the very first pennies I make, I’ll buy Father a new
cloth coat. Cloth, did I say? No, it shall be of gold and silver with
diamond buttons. That poor man certainly deserves it; for, after all,
isn’t he in his shirt sleeves because he was good enough to buy a
book for me? On this cold day, too! Fathers are indeed good to their
children!”

As he talked to himself, he thought he heard sounds of pipes and drums
coming from a distance: pi-pi-pi, pi-pi-pi. . .zum, zum, zum, zum.

He stopped to listen. Those sounds came from a little street that led to
a small village along the shore.

“What can that noise be? What a nuisance that I have to go to school!
Otherwise. . .”

There he stopped, very much puzzled. He felt he had to make up his mind
for either one thing or another. Should he go to school, or should he
follow the pipes?

“Today I’ll follow the pipes, and tomorrow I’ll go to school. There’s
always plenty of time to go to school,” decided the little rascal at
last, shrugging his shoulders.

No sooner said than done. He started down the street, going like the
wind. On he ran, and louder grew the sounds of pipe and drum: pi-pi-pi,
pi-pi-pi, pi-pi-pi . . .zum, zum, zum, zum.

Suddenly, he found himself in a large square, full of people standing in
front of a little wooden building painted in brilliant colors.

“What is that house?” Pinocchio asked a little boy near him.

“Read the sign and you’ll know.”

“I’d like to read, but somehow I can’t today.”

observed.input_line: My sister is covering my chores for a course I'm taking; I picture making it up to her when I qualify, but I keep wasting the study evenings she gives me. Can you help me work out one small way to honour her help this week, without turning a missed evening into 'I'm a terrible person'?

context_resolution.explanation: No confirmed book or reading boundary yet; Muse will call librarian_route during its own turn if the request appears to depend on a specific book.

observed.reply:
Try making the honouring act small and specific: send your sister a message this week saying, “I know you’ve been covering my chores so I can take this course, and I really appreciate it. I’m going to use one 25-minute block tonight well—but if I miss it, I’ll reset rather than beat myself up.” Then do one concrete task for her, such as taking back one chore or making her a cup of tea.

That lets you acknowledge her help now instead of making your gratitude depend on qualifying later. A missed evening can be information about what got in the way—not a verdict on your character.

his tears, he jumped on his father’s neck and kissed him over and over.

I didn't note who said it or where he was going. I read in such short bursts that his promises and changes of mind have run together.

evidence.text:
“Today I’ll follow the pipes, and tomorrow I’ll go to school. There’s
always plenty of time to go to school,” decided the little rascal at
last, shrugging his shoulders.

“What do you care about school? You can go there tomorrow. With a lesson
more or less, we are always the same donkeys.”

“Very well, then. Let’s see who gets there first!” cried Pinocchio.

At the signal, the little troop, with books under their arms, dashed
across the fields. Pinocchio led the way, running as if on wings, the
others following as fast as they could.

What was his surprise and his joy when, on looking himself over, he saw
that he was no longer a Marionette, but that he had become a real live
boy!
